eligibility_reason: Contribution 1 defines graph state as 'a deterministic fold over an append-only event log', with behaviors (including LLM-backed routines) that 'react to changes in the graph and emit new events' (p. 2). LLM-backed behaviors write events at run time (e.g. the llm.requested/llm.responded events from the claude-sonnet-4-5-backed question_generator behavior, p. 7) and other behaviors later react to the resulting graph state to decide their own next action (p. 2, p. 9: contradiction detection and memo synthesis react to claims and evidence objects written earlier in the same run). This is a run-time-written, later-retrieved externalised store conditioning future agent behaviour, satisfying I1. Not E1: the paper repeatedly describes cross-step state semantics (replay, forking at any event, lineage) rather than a hardware/context-window optimisation. Not E2/E3: the log and graph are externalised and are continuously written by the agent's own behaviors, not a fixed corpus. Not E4 (primary systems paper), not E6 (LLM-backed behaviors are integral, p. 1-2, p. 7), not E7 (12 pages, full text). Year 2026 (arXiv 2605.21997, p. 1), English, full text present.

facets.justification: The paper's own title and Contribution 1 name the deliberate relationship between two stores as the contribution itself: 'the append-only event log is the source of truth; the working graph is a deterministic projection of that log' (p. 1-2). The graph carries typed nodes/objects and typed edges/relations that behaviors read and write (p. 9: 93 objects, 76 relations), while the log is what is actually persisted and replayed (p. 7-8). This log-to-graph projection relationship, not either store alone, is what §2-§5 argue for.

'The append-only event log is the source of truth' and 'graph state is a deterministic fold over an append-only event log' (Contribution 1, p. 2). Rule changes, tool calls, and produced claims are each modeled as new events rather than as rewrites of existing entries (p. 2).

'Behaviors subscribe to patterns over events and graph shape; when a matching change occurs, the behavior fires' (p. 2) — an exact pattern/structural match over the graph, not a ranking, and not stated as similarity- or recency-based.

The authors state directly: 'This is a systems paper; its contributions are architectural, not empirical claims about task performance' (p. 2), and 'We report no large-scale empirical evaluation of task performance; this is a systems and architecture contribution' (p. 11). The worked diligence example (§6, p. 8-9) argues the design with a demonstration but is explicitly not a systematic evaluation against baselines.

The diligence pack run is reported as event/object/relation counts and reproducibility (byte-identical replay) rather than a comparison against any baseline or condition (p. 8-9): 'the quantitative artifacts we present ... are demonstrations of the mechanism rather than a benchmark study' (p. 11).

The paper offers a runtime/architecture for organising agentic systems around an event-sourced graph (Contribution 1, p. 2), open-sourced as activegraph (p. 1 footnote), but the paper explicitly argues for the architecture itself ('the substrate and its guarantees', p. 2) rather than for the released package as an end in itself.
